# Kai Gao

I am a 6th year PhD student in economics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, specializing in industrial organization and environmental economics. My research studies how regulation changes consumer behavior and firms' product design.

I am on the academic job market in 2026–27.

## Working Papers {#working-papers}

::: {.paper}
### Beyond the Label: Do Ecodesign Regulations Reduce Real-World Energy Use? (Job Market Paper) {#beyond-the-label-do-ecodesign-regulations-reduce-real-world-energy-use-jmp}

[Paper (PDF)](files/Gao_JMP.pdf)


<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>

<p>
This paper studies how ecodesign regulation shapes product design and consumer welfare when compliance is tied to a single operating mode rather than overall use. I examine the German washing machine market following the 2021 EU reform, which rescaled energy labels based on Eco-program efficiency and capped the program’s duration to make Eco washes more convenient for consumers. Combining detailed product and wash-program data with an original household survey, I find that consumers prefer higher energy-efficiency ratings, yet use Eco for only about 10 percent of their wash cycles. Survey responses indicate that many interpret the label as measuring whole-machine efficiency. Meanwhile, firms offer more energy-efficient Eco programs but more energy-intensive Cotton programs. To explain these responses, I develop an equilibrium model of product entry and program design and estimate it using a novel approach combining composite conditional likelihood with Gibbs sampling, obtaining estimates comparable to those from full portfolio likelihood without enumerating each firm’s large portfolio choice set. The estimates indicate that the duration cap shifts households that value cleaning performance toward Cotton programs, as shorter Eco cycles clean less thoroughly. This substitution increases firms’ incentives to offer longer, more energy-intensive Cotton cycles. Counterfactual results indicate that, relative to a no-reform benchmark, the 2021 reform increases electricity consumption by 3.12 percent and reduces consumer welfare by \texteuro{}~231.1 million. Broadening the efficiency index to include Cotton programs can further increase consumer surplus and reduce electricity expenditure. 
</p>

</details>

:::

::: {.paper}
### What Drives the Repowering of Wind Turbines? Evidence from the Danish Wind Energy Industry

I study how renewable-energy subsidies affect the replacement of aging wind turbines in Denmark. A dynamic model of investment and replacement examines how support for existing installations shapes the timing of technology upgrades and evaluates alternative subsidy designs.
:::

## Work in Progress {#work-in-progress}

::: {.paper}
### Fragmented Environmental Regulation in Global Shipping

I study how geographically fragmented sulfur regulation shapes carriers' vessel deployment, routing, and technology investment. Combining vessel characteristics and pollution-control technology records with AIS movements and freight rates, I examine responses to the 2020 tightening of the global fuel-sulfur limit. I am developing an equilibrium model to compare the welfare effects of regional sulfur standards, voyage-based pollution taxes, and vessel-based requirements.
:::
